title: Idempotency, dedupe and hashing
summary: Idempotent ingestion gives the same index state however many times a change is delivered. It rests on stable ids, normalised content hashes and a deliberate rule for duplicates.
useIf: Events, retries or replays can deliver the same document twice, or the same text exists in many copies.
avoidIf: You build one-off loads that never rerun: key design still helps, but the dedupe machinery is overkill.

explain.md: Delivery is at least once almost everywhere: Event Grid, Debezium and your own retries [[tr26]] [[tr25]]. The cure is at the sink. Push `mergeOrUpload` is the usual action for incremental updates, and `delete` on a missing key is safe, so a replayed batch is safe [[tr2]]. That only helps if the **key is stable**: build the document id from an immutable source id (a file id or primary key), never from a path that a rename changes, and never from a random value generated per attempt.

Chunk ids are a design choice. An ordinal id (`doc42-7`) is simple, but inserting a paragraph shifts every later chunk. An id based on the chunk's content hash stays stable for unchanged chunks, so you can reuse their embeddings and only embed the new ones. For per-document replacement, write the new set of chunks, then delete the chunks of that document that are not in the set. Index projections do part of this: projected keys carry a random hash that changes when the parent changes, so stale chunks are replaced, but children of a deleted parent are removed only when the data source has a deletion detection policy [[tr11]].

explain.md: **Normalise before hashing**: Unicode form, whitespace, line endings and volatile boilerplate such as a printed timestamp. **Dedupe with permissions in mind.** Two copies with identical text may carry different ACLs, and dropping one by hash can remove access or expose the wrong copy. Prefer tagging copies with a cluster id and collapsing them at query time, after security trimming.

whereToUse: Any ingestion path with retries, queues or event delivery
Wikis and drives where pages are edited often and renamed or moved
Corpora with many copies of the same policy, template or email thread
Re-embedding jobs that should reuse vectors for unchanged chunks
Backfills that must be safe to restart after a crash

use: Use a stable key from an immutable source id for every document
Use `mergeOrUpload` so replays and retries land on the same document
Use a normalised content hash to skip unchanged items and detect duplicates
Use cluster ids, not deletion, when copies carry different permissions
avoid: Avoid path-based ids when folders get renamed
Avoid random GUIDs minted per attempt, which turn every retry into a duplicate
Avoid fuzzy near-duplicate deletion without human or rule-based review
flips: Documents rarely change and are small: ordinal chunk ids are fine, skip chunk-level hashing
Embedding cost dominates: add chunk-hash reuse so only new chunks are embedded
Copies carry different ACLs: keep every copy and collapse at query time

pitfalls.symptom: Renaming a folder creates duplicate chunks
pitfalls.cause: The document id was built from the path
pitfalls.fix: Use an immutable source id and migrate existing keys once

pitfalls.symptom: A one-line edit re-embeds an entire long page
pitfalls.cause: Chunk ids and embeddings depend on the ordinal position
pitfalls.fix: Hash chunk text and reuse stored vectors for chunks whose hash and model version match

pitfalls.symptom: Unchanged files look changed after export
pitfalls.cause: Whitespace, line endings or a printed date alter the hash
pitfalls.fix: Normalise text and strip volatile boilerplate before hashing

pitfalls.symptom: Top results are five copies of one policy
pitfalls.fix: Cluster copies, collapse after security trimming and keep each copy's ACL

scenarios.title: Large wiki pages with frequent small edits
scenarios.situation: A wiki has pages of about 100 chunks. Editors change a sentence or add a paragraph near the top many times a day. Embedding spend is a concern and replays happen after failures.
unknowns: Is an immutable page id available?
How often is the embedding model changed?
scenarios.question: How do you key and update chunks?

options.name: Immutable page id for documents, chunk ids from chunk hashes, replace per page and reuse unchanged vectors
options.why: Edits embed only new chunks, renames do not orphan data and replays are safe.
options.tradeoff: A hash store, per-page replacement logic and the model version in the hash input.

options.name: Ordinal chunk ids, re-embed the whole page on any edit
options.tradeoff: Pays for about 100 embeddings on a one-word change.

options.name: Random GUID per chunk per run
options.why: Every retry or replay adds new copies.
options.tradeoff: Only harmless for a single non-repeating load.

flips.then: Ordinal ids with full re-embed cost little.
Cached vectors are invalid, so rebuild into a new index.

scenarios.takeaway: Stable ids make replays safe, and chunk hashes make edits cheap.

scenarios.title: Twelve departmental copies of one policy
scenarios.situation: A shared drive holds identical or near-identical copies of a policy in twelve departments. Each copy has its own permissions. Answers keep citing five copies of the same text.
unknowns: Are the copies bit-identical or edited?
Is a user allowed to see a copy that sits in another department?
scenarios.question: How do you handle the duplicates?

options.name: Keep each copy with its own ACL, add a cluster id and collapse at query time after trimming
options.why: Callers see one result per cluster from copies they may read, and no permission is lost.
options.tradeoff: More chunks stored and a collapse step in retrieval.

options.name: Exact-hash dedupe within the same ACL scope only
options.why: Removes true duplicates safely inside one permission group.

options.name: Global dedupe by hash keeping the first copy
options.why: Users who cannot read the kept copy lose the answer, or the wrong ACL governs it.
options.tradeoff: Right only when all copies share one permission scope.

flips.if: Every copy has the same permissions
flips.then: Global dedupe by normalised hash is simple and safe.
Treat them as distinct documents and rely on reranking.

scenarios.takeaway: Dedupe is a retrieval and security decision, not only a storage one.

quiz.q: After a folder rename, search shows duplicate chunks for the same file. What is the most likely cause?
options: Document ids were built from the file path
quiz.explain: A path-based id changes on rename, so the upsert creates a new document and the old one remains. The other options do not generate duplicate documents.

quiz.q: Which steps belong before computing a content hash used for change detection?
options: Strip volatile boilerplate such as a printed timestamp
Add a random salt per run
Use the same normalisation in every pipeline version
quiz.explain: Hashes only help if equal content gives equal hashes, so normalise, strip volatility and keep rules stable. A random salt makes every hash differ.

quiz.q: Two copies of a document have identical text but different ACLs. What is the safest dedupe approach?
options: Delete the second copy by hash
Merge both ACLs into the first copy
Keep both with a cluster id and collapse at query time after security trimming
Drop the ACL fields to save space
quiz.explain: Collapsing after trimming preserves each copy's permissions. Deleting or merging can hide answers or widen access, and dropping ACL fields breaks trimming.

flashcards.front: What makes a replayed push batch safe?
flashcards.back: `mergeOrUpload` with stable keys, and `delete` on a missing key being safe. The same batch lands on the same documents.

flashcards.front: Why use an immutable source id for the document key?
flashcards.back: Paths change on rename or move, which would orphan old chunks and create duplicates.

flashcards.front: Why include the embedding model version in a chunk-hash cache key?
flashcards.back: A stored vector is only valid for its model. A different model needs new vectors even for identical text.
